slide.title: Which Customers Cost You?
slide.body: Two plates: one normal with a green coin stack, one overflowing with a red minus sign. Small tag: Building an AI Startup · Lesson 9.

scenes.voiceover: A traditional app costs almost nothing extra when one more customer uses it. An AI product is different. Every time a customer presses the button, you pay the model supplier. So do you know which of your customers are making you money?

slide.title: Unit Economics of an AI Product
slide.body: Building an AI Startup · Lesson 9 of 15

scenes.voiceover: Last time, you made the AI part reliable. Now we check that it can pay for itself. Unit economics means looking at the money for one unit of your business, usually one customer per month. How much does one customer bring in, and how much does it cost to serve them?

slide.title: Revenue vs cost to serve
slide.body: Left: Revenue per customer (monthly plan price). Right: Cost to serve = model usage + hosting and tools + support + payment fees.

scenes.voiceover: Revenue per customer is what they pay you, such as a monthly plan. Cost to serve is everything you spend because that customer uses the product. Model usage, which suppliers usually charge by the amount of text processed. Your share of hosting and tools. Support time. And payment fees.

slide.title: Two formulas
slide.body: Gross profit = revenue − cost to serve / Gross margin = gross profit ÷ revenue × 100%

scenes.voiceover: Gross profit is revenue minus cost to serve. Gross margin is gross profit as a percentage of revenue. It shows how much of each unit of money you keep, to pay for salaries, marketing and rent.

slide.title: CAC and payback
slide.body: CAC = marketing and sales spend ÷ new customers / Payback period (months) = CAC ÷ monthly gross profit per customer

scenes.voiceover: Two more terms. CAC, or customer acquisition cost, is what you spend on marketing and sales to win one new customer. The payback period is how many months of gross profit it takes to earn that back.

scenes.stock_query: guests at buffet restaurant filling plates
scenes.voiceover: Think of an all you can eat restaurant. The price is fixed, but the cost depends on how much each guest eats. Most guests are profitable. A few very hungry guests cost more than they pay. The owner must know both before setting the price.

scenes.stock_query: small guesthouse courtyard with host at desk
scenes.voiceover: Let's do the maths. Karim is a made up founder in Marrakech, Morocco. His product drafts replies to guest messages for small guesthouses. All the prices here are placeholders, not real prices. Always check current prices on the day you calculate.

slide.title: Average customer (placeholder prices)
slide.body: Table. Plan: $20/month. Model: 600 × $0.004 = $2.40 · Hosting and tools: $1.50 · Support: $2.00 · Payment fee 3% of $20: $0.60 · Total cost to serve: $6.50.

scenes.voiceover: Karim charges twenty dollars a month. An average customer sends six hundred requests, at four tenths of a cent each. That is two dollars forty. Add one dollar fifty for hosting, two dollars for support, and a three percent payment fee, which is sixty cents. The total cost to serve is six dollars fifty.

slide.title: Average customer: margin
slide.body: Gross profit = $20.00 − $6.50 = $13.50 / Gross margin = $13.50 ÷ $20.00 = 67.5%. Label: Placeholder prices.

scenes.voiceover: So gross profit is twenty dollars minus six dollars fifty, which is thirteen dollars fifty a month. And the gross margin is thirteen fifty divided by twenty. That is sixty seven point five percent. So far, so good.

slide.title: Heavy user (placeholder prices)
slide.body: Model: 5,000 × $0.004 = $20.00 · + hosting $1.50 + support $2.00 + fee $0.60 = $24.10 cost to serve. Revenue $20.00 → loss −$4.10 per month (red).

scenes.voiceover: Now the heavy user. One large guesthouse sends five thousand requests a month. Model usage alone becomes twenty dollars. The total cost to serve becomes twenty four dollars ten. Karim loses four dollars ten on this customer, every month.

slide.title: CAC and payback
slide.body: CAC = $300 ÷ 10 customers = $30 / Payback = $30 ÷ $13.50 per month ≈ 2.2 months. Label: Placeholder prices.

scenes.voiceover: Finally, CAC and payback. Karim spent three hundred dollars on local advertising and won ten customers. So his CAC is thirty dollars. Thirty divided by thirteen fifty gives a payback period of about two point two months. An average customer must stay more than two months before he earns back the cost of winning them.

slide.title: Karim's decisions
slide.body: Usage limit on the $20 plan (for example 1,500 requests) · Higher-priced plan for large guesthouses · Shorter prompts, lower model cost per request

scenes.voiceover: So Karim makes three decisions. He adds a usage limit to the twenty dollar plan. He creates a higher priced plan for large guesthouses. And he shortens his prompts to reduce model usage per request.
The common mistake is calculating only the average user. With AI, a few heavy users can remove your profit. Always calculate at least two cases, and do not forget support and payment fees.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Revenue vs cost to serve, per customer. 2. Gross margin; heavy users can lose money. 3. CAC and payback period.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, unit economics compares what one customer pays with what it costs to serve them. Second, gross margin is gross profit divided by revenue, and heavy AI usage can make a cheap plan lose money. Third, CAC and payback show how long a customer must stay before you earn back the cost of winning them.

Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, estimate the monthly cost and revenue per customer for your MVP in a free spreadsheet, for an average and a heavy user. Then ask Claude to check your formulas. Next, we look at choosing a business model. See you there.
